```{python}
        y=np.maximum(shortfall, 1e-4),
        mode="lines",
        name=f"DP sweeps, {label}",
        line=dict(color=colors[i], width=2, dash="dot"),
        hovertemplate="<b>%{y:.3f}</b> steps",
        row=1, col=1
    )

rtdp_fig.add_scatter(
    x=updates_rtdp,
    y=np.maximum(np.median(shortfall_rtdp, axis=1), 1e-4),
    mode="lines",
    name=f"RTDP (median of {N_RUNS_RTDP} runs)",
    line=dict(color=colors[3], width=3),
    hovertemplate="<b>%{y:.3f}</b> steps",
    row=1, col=1
)

rtdp_fig.add_heatmap(
    z=np.log10(1 + updates_per_cell),
    customdata=updates_per_cell,
    colorscale="Teal",
    colorbar=dict(title="Updates (log10)", x=1.0, len=0.9),
    hovertemplate="row: %{y}<br>col: %{x}<br>%{customdata:,.1f} updates (averaged over runs)<extra></extra>",
    row=1, col=2
)

rtdp_fig.update_xaxes(title_text="updates", row=1, col=1)
rtdp_fig.update_yaxes(title_text="expected extra steps (log scale)", type="log", exponentformat="power",
                      row=1, col=1)
rtdp_fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, showgrid=False, zeroline=False, row=1, col=2)
rtdp_fig.update_yaxes(
    autorange="reversed",
    showticklabels=False,
    showgrid=False,
    zeroline=False,
    row=1, col=2
)
rtdp_fig.update_layout(
    title="RTDP vs sweeping value iteration on the racetrack",
    template="plotly_dark",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.15, x=0),
    margin=dict(t=100, b=100)
)

rtdp_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))
```

Random-order DP needs **28 sweeps** to meet its stopping rule. RTDP leaves most states almost untouched: **92% were updated at most 100 times, and 73% at most 10 times** (the book: 98% and 81%), and 0.7% were never updated at all (the book: 3.2%).

The heat map on the right shows where RTDP's updates went, and it has a striking stripe pattern. On the long straight the car travels three or four cells per step, so it only ever *lands* on every third or fourth row. Those rows get five to eight times as many updates as the rows it flies over. In the turn, the cells the car swings through get thousands of updates, while the far-left corner of the top section gets none at all.

**How much computation each method needed** for this experiment does not agree with the book.

- **By the book's criteria, RTDP wins.** DP's stopping rule (no value changes by more than $10^{-4}$ in a sweep) is met after 76,244 updates. RTDP's greedy policy gets within 0.1 expected steps of optimal after a median of 45,000 updates (2,670 episodes). This is the book's kind of comparison - DP run until its convergence test passes, RTDP run until its performance stops improving - and by it RTDP needs about 60% of the updates.

- **According to the oracle, DP was actually done much earlier.** DP's greedy policy was within 0.1 steps of optimal after 32,000 updates, less than halfway to its own stopping rule, and DP is ahead of RTDP at every tolerance. The two stopping rules measure different things. DP's measures its *values*, which keep changing long after the *policy* has stopped changing; RTDP's measures its policy. Without an oracle, neither method could see the other's number.

- **RTDP doesn't save more because so many states are relevant.** On our track, 48% of the reachable states are relevant. In the book's example it is 599 of 9,115, under 7%. RTDP's advantage comes from skipping the states that no optimal policy needs, and our track has comparatively few of them to skip. A track with a large region that good driving never enters would favor RTDP more.

**The convergence theorem does hold.** After 150,000 updates, RTDP's median shortfall is $0.007$ steps, and only 0.08% of the *relevant* states were never updated, against 1.2% of the irrelevant ones. Even so, 2 of the 10 runs still hadn't reached a shortfall of 0.01. RTDP's final stretch is slow, because it has to pin down the values of rarely visited states well enough to tell nearly tied actions apart.

# Planning at decision time

Every planner so far has done **background planning**. It gradually improves a table of values (or a policy) for *all* states, and when the agent finds itself in a state, it simply looks up the action in the table. DP, Dyna, prioritized sweeping and RTDP all work this way. None of their planning is about the current state in particular.

**Decision-time planning**, on the contrary, is when the agent reaches a state $S_t$, it starts planning *from that state*, produces a single action $A_t$, and then usually throws the planning away. At the next state it starts again from scratch. The values it computes are about one state, and are used **once**. This makes sense when the agent doesn't have to respond instantly (e.g. a chess program can think for several seconds per move) and it lets the agent spend far more computation on the current decision.

The next three sections cover three different ways to do decision time planning. To compare them fairly, they all get the same problem and **the same weak starting knowledge**.

Here we will reuse the cliff environment, with $\gamma = 0.95$. The discount is needed because the rollout methods have to cut their simulations off at some point. Without discounting, a random walk on the cliff takes tens of thousands of steps to finish. With $\gamma = 0.95$, cutting a return off after 150 steps changes it by at most $0.95^{150}\cdot|v| \approx 0.14$.

**The starting knowledge** is the uniformly random policy. Methods that need values get its value function, $v_{\text{random}}$, whereas methods that need to simulate get the policy itself.

## How to grade a decision-time planner

A decision-time planner doesn't store a table, so there is nothing to compare with $q_*$ directly. But it does *define* a policy: in state $s$, the probability that the planner, run from scratch, with fresh random numbers, returns action $a$. And because the planner starts from scratch at every step, that probability depends only on the current state. In other words the policy is Markov, so the DP oracle can evaluate it exactly.

So we run each planner $K$ times from every state, count how often it picks each action to get an empirical $\pi(a\mid s)$, and pass that policy to `exact` to get $v_\pi$. That gives us three evaluation metrics:

- $v_\pi(S)$, the value at the start state
- the **mean shortfall** $\frac1{37}\sum_s\left[v_*(s) - v_\pi(s)\right]$: how far below optimal the policy is, averaged over the 37 states the agent can be in
- **optimal choices**: the probability the planner puts on optimal actions, averaged over those same states.


```{python}
GAMMA_CLIFF = 0.95
start_cliff = int(np.argmax(cliff.start))
live_cliff = cliff.reachable & ~cliff.terminal
roots_cliff = np.flatnonzero(live_cliff) # every state a decision is made in
n_rows_cliff, n_cols_cliff = cliff.shape
cliff_cells = [(n_rows_cliff - 1) * n_cols_cliff + col for col in range(1, n_cols_cliff - 1)]
v_star_cliff, q_star_cliff = exact(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF)
pi_random = np.ones((cliff.n_states, cliff.n_actions)) / cliff.n_actions
v_random, q_random = exact(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF, pi_random)
optimal_cliff = q_star_cliff >= v_star_cliff[:, None] - TIE_TOLERANCE  # the optimal actions of each state

def induced_policy(actions, roots, env):
    """Turn the actions a planner chose into a policy table pi(a|s).

    A decision-time planner is run several times from each state. The induced policy picks
    each action with the fraction of those runs that chose it. In states where the planner
    was never run, it is uniform.

    Parameters
    ----------
    actions : array_like of int, shape (n_calls,)
        The action chosen by each planner call.
    roots : array_like of int, shape (n_calls,)
        The state each call planned from.
    env : Env
        Supplies the table sizes.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        pi(a|s). Each row sums to 1.
    """
    pi = np.zeros((env.n_states, env.n_actions))
    np.add.at(pi, (roots, actions), 1.0)
    pi[pi.sum(axis=1) == 0] = 1.0 / env.n_actions # Uniform
    return pi / pi.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

def greedy_ties_split(q, env):
    """Return the greedy policy of q, with ties split evenly.

    An action is tied for best when its value is within TIE_TOLERANCE of the largest legal
    value. Each tied action gets an equal share of the probability.

    Parameters
    ----------
    q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Action values.
    env : Env
        Supplies the legal actions.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        pi(a|s). Each row sums to 1.
    """
    q_legal = np.where(env.legal_actions > 0, q, NEG_INF)
    best = q_legal >= q_legal.max(axis=1, keepdims=True) - TIE_TOLERANCE
    return best / best.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

def grade(pi):
    """Grade a policy on the cliff exactly, with the DP oracle.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pi : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The policy, as pi(a|s).

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        - "start": v_pi(S), the value of the start state.
        - "shortfall": the mean over the live states of v_*(s) - v_pi(s). 0 is optimal.
        - "optimal": the mean over the live states of the probability pi puts on optimal
          actions. 1 is optimal.
    """
    v, _ = exact(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF, pi)
    return dict(
        start=v[start_cliff],
        shortfall=(v_star_cliff - v)[live_cliff].mean(),
        optimal=(pi * optimal_cliff).sum(axis=1)[live_cliff].mean()
    )


```


```{python}
greedy_random = greedy_ties_split(q_random, cliff)
grades_cliff = pd.DataFrame([
    dict(policy="The random policy", **grade(pi_random)),
    dict(policy="Greedy one-step lookahead on *v*<sub>random</sub>", **grade(greedy_random)),
    dict(policy="Optimal", **grade(greedy_pi(q_star_cliff, cliff))),
])
row_optimal = [len(grades_cliff) - 1]

grades_table = (
    GT(grades_cliff, rowname_col="policy")
    .tab_header(
        title=md("**The starting knowledge, graded exactly on the cliff**"),
        subtitle=f"γ = {GAMMA_CLIFF}. Averages are over the {live_cliff.sum()} states the agent can be in."
    )
    .tab_stubhead(label="Policy")
    .cols_label(
        start=html("<i>v</i><sub>π</sub>(S)"),
        shortfall="Mean shortfall",
        optimal="Optimal choices"
    )
    .fmt_markdown(columns="policy")
    .fmt_number(columns=["start", "shortfall"], decimals=2)
    .fmt_percent(columns="optimal", decimals=1)
    .cols_align("right", columns=["start", "shortfall", "optimal"])
    .tab_style(style.text(color="gray", style="italic"), loc.body(rows=row_optimal))
    .tab_style(style.text(color="gray", style="italic"), loc.stub(rows=row_optimal))
    .tab_footnote(
        "The value of the start state S. Higher is better.",
        loc.column_labels(columns="start")
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        html("The mean of <i>v</i><sub>*</sub>(s) − <i>v</i><sub>π</sub>(s). 0 is optimal; lower is better."),
        loc.column_labels(columns="shortfall")
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        "The mean probability the policy puts on optimal actions. 100% is optimal.",
        loc.column_labels(columns="optimal")
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        "One step of policy iteration. Actions tied for best share the probability equally.",
        loc.stub(rows=[1])
    )
    .tab_source_note(md("Every value comes from the DP oracle (`exact`), not from sampled episodes."))
)
grades_table
```

```{python}
policy_figure(
```

**The random policy in this experiment is terrible:** $v(S) = -261$, because along the bottom row a quarter of its moves step off the cliff.

**One step of greedy lookahead on its values** (which is one step of policy iteration) is an enormous improvement, bringing it up to $-20$. But look at what that policy actually *does* (the top panel of the figure above). On the left half of the board it walks up into the top-left corner, whereas on the right half it runs along the top row into the top-right corner, and in both places it stays, pushing into the wall forever. $-20 = -1/(1-0.95)$ is exactly the value of never finishing; $-1$ on every step, discounted forever. Only the four cells beside the goal actually lead into it.

**The issue is $v_{\text{random}}$ itself.** Under the random policy the goal is so far away that it barely affects the values, while the cliff dominates every state near it. So the values effectively say, *get away from the cliff*. The one-step lookahead does exactly that, and hides in a corner. The knowledge the planners start from is actively misleading, and each decision-time planner has to overcome it by looking ahead.

:::{.callout-warning}
`greedy_ties_split` gives actions that are exactly tied for best equal probability, as the Dyna agents did, rather than handing every tie to action 0. With one step of lookahead only two states have ties, so it barely matters yet. But it will in later sections.
:::

# Heuristic search

Heuristic search is the classic decision-time planner. From the current state, it builds a **tree** of every possible continuation, out to some depth $d$. At the leaves of the tree, it uses an approximate value function $V$ (the *heuristic*) as its guess of what happens after that. Then it backs the values up toward the root: at each of its own decisions it takes the max over actions, and wherever the environment is random it takes the expectation over outcomes (the cliff is deterministic, so there are none of those here). Finally it picks the best action at the root and throws the tree away.

The key point is that the value backed up to the root is exactly what $d$ steps of value iteration starting from $V$ would result in. Deeper search helps because each extra level of lookahead is one more value-iteration step, so whatever error $V$ has is shrunk by one more factor of $\gamma$ before it reaches the root. The difference from background value iteration is *where* the
computation goes. Search spends it *only* on the current state and the states reachable from it, whereas value iteration spreads it over every state.

## The tree, level by level

With 4 actions and only deterministic moves, the states at depth $k$ of the tree, for every root, fit in an array of shape `(n_roots, 4^k)`. Building the next level is one lookup in the successor table followed by a reshape. To back up a level we add the rewards then reshape to `(n_roots, 4^{k-1}, 4)` so that each node's four children sit together, and take the max over the last axis.

There is no `scan` here, because a `scan` needs every step to have the same shape, and each level of the tree has a different one. So the loop over levels is an ordinary Python loop that builds the graph one level at a time, and the depth $d$ is fixed when the function is built.


```{python}
def make_heuristic_search(env, depth, V_leaf, gamma):
    """Compile an exhaustive depth-d lookahead tree, for a batch of roots in a deterministic env.

    The tree holds every action sequence of length ``depth`` from the root, n_actions^depth
    leaves in all. Each leaf is valued by the heuristic ``V_leaf``. Values are then backed
    up one level at a time, toward the root:

        value(node) = max over legal a of [ r(node, a) + gamma * value(child after a) ].

    At the root the max is not taken, so the root keeps one backed-up value per action.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        A deterministic environment. Its next state is read as ``P.argmax(axis=2)``.
    depth : int
        Number of levels of actions in the tree. 1 is the one-step lookahead.
    V_leaf : ndarray, shape (n_states,)
        The heuristic value of each state, used at the leaves.
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``f(roots) -> (best_action, root_values)``, with ``roots`` of shape (n_roots,).
        ``best_action`` has shape (n_roots,) and ``root_values`` (n_roots, n_actions).
    """
    next_state = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.P.argmax(axis=2))
    reward = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.reward_mean)
    legal = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.legal_actions)
    V = pt.as_tensor_variable(V_leaf)
    roots = pt.lvector("roots")
    n_roots = roots.shape[0]

    levels = [roots[:, None]] # (n_roots, 1), (n_roots, 4), (n_roots, 16) ...
    for _ in range(depth):
        levels.append(next_state[levels[-1]].reshape((n_roots, -1)))

    value = V[levels[-1]] # the heuristic, at the leaves
    for k in range(depth - 1, -1, -1): # back up one level at a time
        s = levels[k]
        backed_up_values = reward[s] + gamma * value.reshape((n_roots, -1, env.n_actions))
        backed_up_values = pt.where(legal[s] > 0, backed_up_values, NEG_INF)
        value = backed_up_values.max(axis=-1) if k > 0 else backed_up_values[:, 0, :]
    return pytensor.function([roots], [value.argmax(axis=-1), value])

def lookahead_by_value_iteration(V, depth):
    """Compute the depth-d tree's root values without building the tree, on the cliff.

    A depth-d tree backs up d levels from V. That is the same as d - 1 sweeps of value
    iteration starting from V, followed by one more one-step lookahead
    ``q(s, a) = r(s, a) + gamma * v(s')`` that keeps every action. This gives the root
    values for every state at once, at a cost that grows with d instead of 4^d.

    Parameters
    ----------
    V : ndarray, shape (n_states,)
        The heuristic value of each state.
    depth : int
        The depth of the tree being reproduced.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The backed-up value of each action from each state, as the root of a depth-d tree.
    """
    _, _, action_values_of = ORACLE[cliff.name]
    v = V.copy()
    for _ in range(depth - 1):
        v = np.where(cliff.terminal, 0.0, action_values_of(v, GAMMA_CLIFF).max(axis=1))
    return action_values_of(v, GAMMA_CLIFF)

```


```{python}
check_rows = []
for depth in (1, 2, 4, 6, 8):
    search = make_heuristic_search(cliff, depth, v_random, GAMMA_CLIFF)
    _, root_values = search(roots_cliff)
    difference = np.abs(root_values - lookahead_by_value_iteration(v_random, depth)[roots_cliff]).max()
    check_rows.append(dict(depth=depth, leaves=cliff.n_actions ** depth, difference=difference))
tree_check = pd.DataFrame(check_rows)

tree_check_table = (
    GT(tree_check, rowname_col="depth")
    .tab_header(
        title=md("**The literal tree vs. value iteration, on the cliff**"),
        subtitle=html(f"Leaves valued by <i>v</i><sub>random</sub>. γ = {GAMMA_CLIFF}. "
                      f"All {len(roots_cliff)} states the agent can be in are searched from at once.")
    )
    .tab_stubhead(label=html("Depth <i>d</i>"))
    .cols_label(
        leaves="Leaves per root",
        difference="Largest difference"
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns="leaves")
    .fmt_scientific(columns="difference", decimals=1)
    .cols_align("right", columns=["leaves", "difference"])
    .tab_footnote(
        html(f"{cliff.n_actions}<sup><i>d</i></sup>: one leaf for every sequence of <i>d</i> actions."),
        loc.column_labels(columns="leaves")
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        f"The largest |tree − value iteration| over all {len(roots_cliff)} roots and all "
        f"{cliff.n_actions} root actions. 0.0 means the two agree to the last bit.",
        loc.column_labels(columns="difference")
    )

tree_check_table
```

The tree and value iteration agree exactly at every depth. So from here on we can use whichever form is cheaper. The check above built trees for all 37 roots at once, up to depth 8 (2.4 million leaves in total). The table below uses the value-iteration form at every depth, and as a spot check we also build two literal trees from the start state alone: depth 11 and depth 12,
with 4.2 and 16.8 million leaves.

On the cliff every step costs $-1$, which produces many tied actions. So the policy at each depth splits its probability evenly between the tied best actions (`greedy_ties_split`), just as the Dyna agents did.


```{python}
ARROW_GLYPHS = {UP: "↑", DOWN: "↓", LEFT: "←", RIGHT: "→"}   # the four actions, drawn as arrows for tables

def per_action(values):
    """Format one value per action as "↑ −9.73, ↓ −10.25, ...", with a true minus sign."""
    return ", ".join(f"{ARROW_GLYPHS[a]} {v:.2f}".replace("-", "−") for a, v in enumerate(values))

graded_depth = {}
depth_rows = []
for depth in range(1, 15):
    q_lookahead = lookahead_by_value_iteration(v_random, depth)
    pi_lookahead = greedy_ties_split(q_lookahead, cliff)
    graded_depth[depth] = grade(pi_lookahead)
    in_tree = np.zeros(cliff.n_states, dtype=bool)
    frontier = np.array([start_cliff])

    for _ in range(depth):
        frontier = np.unique(cliff.P.argmax(axis=2)[frontier].ravel())
        in_tree[frontier] = True

    depth_rows.append(dict(
        depth=depth,
        leaves=cliff.n_actions ** depth,
        distinct=in_tree.sum(),
        tied=" ".join(ARROW_GLYPHS[a] for a in np.flatnonzero(pi_lookahead[start_cliff])),
        **graded_depth[depth]
    ))
search_by_depth = pd.DataFrame(depth_rows)

literal_trees = {} # depth -> the backed-up value of each action at S, from the literal tree
for depth in (11, 12):
    _, root_values = make_heuristic_search(cliff, depth, v_random, GAMMA_CLIFF)(np.array([start_cliff]))
    literal_trees[depth] = root_values[0]

row_of_depth = lambda depth: [search_by_depth.index[search_by_depth["depth"] == depth][0]]
search_by_depth_table = (
    GT(search_by_depth, rowname_col="depth")
    .tab_header(
        title=md("**Heuristic search on the cliff, depth by depth**"),
        subtitle=html(f"Leaves valued by <i>v</i><sub>random</sub>. Actions tied for best share the "
                      f"probability equally. γ = {GAMMA_CLIFF}.")
    )
    .tab_stubhead(label=html("Depth <i>d</i>"))
    .tab_spanner(label=html("The tree from <i>S</i>"), columns=["leaves", "distinct", "tied"])
    .tab_spanner(label="The policy, graded exactly", columns=["start", "shortfall", "optimal"])
    .cols_label(
        leaves="Leaves",
        distinct="Distinct states",
        tied=html("Tied best at <i>S</i>"),
        start=html("<i>v</i><sub>π</sub>(S)"),
        shortfall="Mean shortfall",
        optimal="Optimal choices"
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns=["leaves", "distinct"])
    .fmt_number(columns=["start", "shortfall"], decimals=2)
    .fmt_percent(columns="optimal", decimals=1)
    .cols_align("right", columns=["leaves", "distinct", "start", "shortfall", "optimal"])
    .cols_align("center", columns="tied")
    .tab_footnote(
        html(f"The literal depth-11 tree from <i>S</i> ({cliff.n_actions ** 11:,} leaves) backs up "
             f"{per_action(literal_trees[11])}."),
        loc.body(columns="tied", rows=row_of_depth(11))
    )
    .tab_footnote(
        html(f"The literal depth-12 tree from <i>S</i> ({cliff.n_actions ** 12:,} leaves) backs up "
             f"{per_action(literal_trees[12])}."),
        loc.body(columns="tied", rows=row_of_depth(12))
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        "Every row uses the value-iteration form of the tree. Evaluations come from the DP oracle."
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        html(f"For comparison, the optimal action values at <i>S</i>: <i>q</i><sub>*</sub>(S, ·) = "
             f"{per_action(q_star_cliff[start_cliff])}.")
    )
)
search_by_depth_table
```

- **Each extra level of lookahead helps, starting with the states nearest the goal.** The mean shortfall falls as we increase depth, as expected. The first states to be fixed are the ones closest to the goal. A depth-$d$ tree from a state within $d$ steps of the goal can *see* the goal, and once it can, the leaf values' fear of the cliff no longer decides anything. The start state is 13 steps from the goal, the farthest of all, so it is fixed last.

- From depth 4 to depth 11, "up", "down" and "left" at $S$ all back up to *exactly* the same value (the literal depth-11 tree gives $-90.08$ for all three). Every step on the cliff costs $-1$, so a plan that wastes a step now and a plan that wastes a step later reach the same leaf with the same total. Until the tree reaches the cell above the goal (12 steps from $S$), wasting a step costs nothing the tree can see. At depth 12 it can, and "up" pulls clearly ahead with $-61.72$ against $-86.58$. This is why tie-breaking is really important here. Had we broken ties toward action 0, which happens to be "up", depth 11 would have *appeared* to solve the start state when it had only guessed right. Splitting ties shows the real, gradual improvement instead, as more and more of the states downstream of $S$ get fixed.

- **The cost grows exponentially.** Depth 12 means 16.8 million leaves for a single decision, in a world with only 37 states. The tree visits the same states over and over, whereas value iteration merges them: it computed the same numbers for *all* 37 states in 11 sweeps. That is the downside of heuristic search on a tabular problem. It pays off when the state space is too big to sweep but the tree from the current state is still affordable. When the whole table fits in memory, as it does here, search loses.

# Rollout algorithms

A **rollout algorithm** estimates action values by simulation instead of looking them up in a stored $V$. From the current state, for each action $a$, it simulates many trajectories, by taking $a$, then following a fixed **rollout policy** $\pi$ until the episode ends (or, here, until 150 steps have passed). Each trajectory gives one return, and the average of those returns is the estimate of how good $a$ is. The algorithm picks the action with the highest estimate and throws everything else away.

The average return of "take $a$, then follow $\pi$" is exactly $q_\pi(s, a)$. So with enough rollouts, the algorithm acts greedily with respect to $q_\pi$. By the policy improvement theorem that policy is *at least as good as $\pi$*, and it is precisely **one step of policy iteration** starting from $\pi$. A rollout algorithm improves on its rollout policy, but on its own it does not reach the optimal policy. As the book puts it, the aim is to improve upon the rollout policy, not to find an optimal one.

We batch everything. There is one trajectory for each root state, each of the 4 first actions, and each of the $n$ rollouts, which makes an array of `(n_roots, 4, n)` trajectories. A single `scan` over the 150-step horizon moves them all forward together, and each step is one draw from the sample model.


```{python}
def environment_tensors(env):
    """Wrap the parts of the model that rollouts need as constant tensors.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        The environment.

    Returns
    -------
    P : TensorConstant, shape (n_states, n_actions, n_states)
        Transition probabilities.
    reward : TensorConstant, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Expected rewards.
    not_terminal : TensorConstant, shape (n_states,)
        1.0 for non-terminal states, 0.0 for terminal ones.
    n_actions : int
        Number of actions.
    """
    return (
        pt.as_tensor_variable(env.P),
        pt.as_tensor_variable(env.reward_mean),
        pt.as_tensor_variable((~env.terminal).astype("float64")),
        env.n_actions
    )

def random_rollout_returns(rng, s, tensors, gamma, horizon):
    """Simulate one episode of the uniform random policy from every state in s.

    The episode is cut off after ``horizon`` steps, and its discounted return is

        G = R_1 + gamma * R_2 + gamma^2 * R_3 + ... ,

    with no reward after a terminal state. Actions are drawn uniformly from all actions
    and next states from the model.

    Parameters
    ----------
    rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
        The random generator state.
    s : TensorVariable of int, any shape
        The start state of each rollout.
    tensors : tuple
        The output of `environment_tensors`.
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.
    horizon : int
        Steps per rollout.

    Returns
    -------
    rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
        The advanced generator.
    G : TensorVariable, same shape as s
        The return of each rollout.
    """
    P, reward, not_terminal, n_actions = tensors

    def step(rng, s, G, discount):
        "one random step: G += gamma^t * R, and the discount becomes gamma^(t + 1)"
        rng, a = rng.integers(0, n_actions, size=s.shape)
        rng, s_next = rng.categorical(p=P[s, a]) # the sample model
        return rng, s_next, G + discount * not_terminal[s] * reward[s, a], discount * gamma

    rng, _, G_seq, _ = pytensor.scan(
        fn=step,
        outputs_info=[rng, s, pt.zeros(s.shape), pt.constant(1.0, dtype="float64")],
        n_steps=horizon,
        return_updates=False
    )
    return rng, G_seq[-1]

def make_rollout_planner(env, gamma, horizon, seed):
    """Compile a rollout planner with the uniform random rollout policy.

    For each root s and each action a, the planner takes a once and then follows the random
    policy, n times. The mean return estimates q_random(s, a):

        q_estimate(s, a) = mean over the n rollouts of [ r(s, a) + gamma * G ].

    The planner picks the action with the largest estimate.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        The environment, used as a sample model.
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.
    horizon : int
        Steps per rollout after the first action.
    seed : int
        Seed for the shared random generator.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``f(roots, n) -> (best_action, q_estimate)``, with ``roots`` of shape (n_roots,) and
        n rollouts per action.
        ``best_action`` has shape (n_roots,) and ``q_estimate`` (n_roots, n_actions).
    """
    P, reward, not_terminal, n_actions = tensors = environment_tensors(env)
    rng_shared = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=seed, name="rng_rollout_planner")
    roots = pt.lvector("roots")
    n_rollouts = pt.iscalar("n")

    first_action = pt.arange(n_actions)[None, :, None] + pt.zeros((roots.shape[0], 1, n_rollouts), dtype="int64")
    s_root = roots[:, None, None] + pt.zeros_like(first_action) # (n_roots, n_actions, n)

    rng, s_1 = rng_shared.categorical(p=P[s_root, first_action]) # take a
    rng, G = random_rollout_returns(rng, s_1, tensors, gamma, horizon) # follow pi

    q_estimate = (reward[s_root, first_action] + gamma * G).mean(axis=-1)

    return pytensor.function(
        [roots, n_rollouts],
        [q_estimate.argmax(axis=-1), q_estimate],
        updates={rng_shared: rng}
    )
```


```{python}
HORIZON, K_ROLLOUT = 150, 10
rollout_planner = make_rollout_planner(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF, HORIZON, seed=810)
roots_repeated = np.repeat(roots_cliff, K_ROLLOUT)

graded_rollout = {}
for n in (1, 4, 16, 64, 256):
    actions, _ = rollout_planner(roots_repeated, n)
    policy_rollout = induced_policy(actions, roots_repeated, cliff) # the last one is kept
    graded_rollout[n] = grade(policy_rollout)

```


```{python}

```

**More rollouts lead to the one-step policy.** As $n$ grows, the rollout planner converges to the policy from the decision time planning section above. $v(S)$ is about $-20$ at every $n$, and the fraction of optimal choices settles at 28.6%, compared to 29.7% for one step of policy iteration. More simulation doesn't take it any further, because what it estimates more and more precisely is $q_{\text{random}}$, and the greedy policy of $q_{\text{random}}$ hides in the corners.

**The shortfall column doesn't fall steadily** because the exact one-step policy hides *deterministically*. In a state where it chooses to push into a wall, it pushes forever. With a finite
$n$, the planner sometimes ranks a different action first just by chance, so its policy is a little random, and on this problem, any randomness in a hiding state eventually walks the agent out of the corner. At $n = 1$ the estimates are so noisy that the policy is nearly the random one, and it inherits the random policy's falls off the cliff. In between, there is just enough noise to escape the corners, which beats both extremes. As $n$ grows further, the noise disappears and the shortfall should return to the exact policy's $11.79$.

A rollout algorithm improves on its rollout policy, here from $-261$ to about $-20$ at $S$. It is a Monte Carlo version of one policy-improvement step, run at decision time, and it gets exactly as far as one step of policy iteration can.

# Monte Carlo tree search

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is a rollout algorithm with a memory. It keeps a **tree** rooted at the current state, which grows by one node with every simulation. The tree stores an estimate of each action's value, and MCTS uses those estimates to steer later simulations toward the moves that have looked best so far. Each iteration has four steps:

1. **Selection.** Starting at the root, walk down through the nodes already in the tree, choosing actions with the **tree policy**. We use UCB, the rule from the bandits chapter, pick the action with the best average return so far plus an exploration bonus, which is larger for actions that have been tried less often. $a = \arg\max_a \left[\frac{W(n,a)}{N(n,a)} + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln \sum_{a'} N(n,a')}{N(n,a)}}\right]$, where $N(n,a)$ is how many times action $a$ has been taken from node $n$, and $W(n,a)$ is the sum of the returns that followed.

2. **Expansion.** On reaching a node that has an action not yet tried, try one of those actions and add the node it leads to.

3. **Simulation.** From that new node, run the **rollout policy** (here, uniformly random) out to the horizon.

4. **Backup.** Send the return back up the path. On every edge the iteration passed through, add one to $N$ and add the discounted return to $W$. Nothing is stored for the rollout part of the trajectory.

When the budget of iterations is used up, the agent plays the root action with the most visits and throws the tree away.

## A tree in fixed-size arrays

A tree is normally built from pointers, with nodes added one at a time, but a `scan` needs arrays whose shapes never change. The way around this is to notice that a tree growing by one node per iteration can never have more than `n_iterations + 1` nodes. So we allocate arrays of that size up front, one tree per root, and fill them in as the tree grows:

- `node_state[tree, m]`: the state at node $m$ of a tree
- `children[tree, m, a]`: the node that action $a$ leads to from node $m$, or $-1$ if that action has not been expanded yet
- `N[tree, m, a]` and `W[tree, m, a]`: the visit count and the summed returns for each edge.

Each of the four steps then becomes an array operation, done for every tree at once:

- **Selection** is an inner `scan` over depth that walks down every tree together. It carries the current node and an `active` flag, which switches off once a tree reaches an unexpanded action or a terminal state, and it outputs the path each tree took.

- **Expansion** writes one new entry into `children` and one into `node_state`.

- **Simulation** reuses `random_rollout_returns` from the previous section.

- **Backup** walks back along the path from the leaf to work out the return seen from each edge, then adds them all in at once with a single `inc_subtensor`. That is safe because a path never uses the same edge twice, and the padding after a path ends only adds zeros.

The exploration constant $c$ has to match the size of the returns, which here range from about $-10$ to
$-350$. We tried $c \in \{30, 100, 300, 1000\}$ and settled on 300.


```{python}
def make_mcts(env, gamma, horizon, max_depth, n_iterations, c, seed):
    """Compile Monte Carlo tree search with UCB, one tree per root.

    Each iteration in every tree at once:

    1. Selection: from the root, follow the tree. At a node with an untried legal action,
       stop and pick one of those at random. Otherwise pick the action with the largest
       upper confidence bound,

           W(m, a) / N(m, a) + c * sqrt( ln(sum_b N(m, b)) / N(m, a) ),

       where N counts visits of edge (m, a) and W sums their returns.
    2. Expansion: add one node for the untried action's next state.
    3. Simulation: a random rollout of ``horizon`` steps from that state.
    4. Backup: add 1 to N and the discounted return from that edge on to W, for every edge
       on the path.

    The trees live in fixed-size arrays with room for ``n_iterations + 1`` nodes, since
    each iteration adds at most one node. Node 0 is the root.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        The environment, used as a sample model.
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.
    horizon : int
        Steps per rollout.
    max_depth : int
        The most selection steps per iteration.
    n_iterations : int
        Iterations per tree.
    c : float
        Exploration constant of the upper confidence bound.
    seed : int
        Seed for the shared random generator.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``f(roots) -> (best_action, N_root, mean_return)``, with ``roots`` of shape
        (n_trees,). ``best_action`` is the most-visited root action, shape (n_trees,).
        ``N_root`` and ``mean_return = W / N`` at the root have shape (n_trees, n_actions).
    """
    P, reward, not_terminal, n_actions = tensors = environment_tensors(env)
    legal = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.legal_actions)
    rng_shared = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=seed, name="rng_mcts")
    roots = pt.lvector("roots")
    n_trees = roots.shape[0]
    capacity = n_iterations + 1
    trees = pt.arange(n_trees)

    def select(rng, node, active, expand_node, expand_action, leaf, children, node_state, N, W):
        """One level of the selection descent, in every tree at once.

        Parameters
        ----------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        node : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The node each tree's descent is at.
        active : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            1.0 while the descent is still going; 0.0 once it has stopped.
        expand_node, expand_action : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The edge to expand, once the descent finds one.
        leaf : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The state the rollout will start from.
        children : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees, capacity, n_actions)
            The node each edge leads to, or -1 if the edge is not in the tree yet.
        node_state : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees, capacity)
            The environment state of each node.
        N, W : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees, capacity, n_actions)
            Visit counts and summed returns of each edge.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, node_next, active, expand_node, expand_action, leaf
            The carried values for the next level.
        node, a : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The edge taken at this level.
        reward : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            Its reward, or 0 if the edge is not on the path.
        on_path : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            1.0 if this level's edge is part of the path.
        expanding : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            1.0 if this level's edge is the one being expanded.
        """
        s = node_state[trees, node]
        at_terminal = 1.0 - not_terminal[s]
        untried = pt.lt(children[trees, node], 0) * legal[s] # -1 for not expanded yet
        has_untried = pt.gt(untried.sum(axis=1), 0)

        # the 1e-12 keeps the probabilities defined when nothing is untried; that draw is then unused
        rng, a_new = rng.categorical(p=(untried + 1e-12) / (untried + 1e-12).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
        visits = N[trees, node]
        ucb = W[trees, node] / visits + c * pt.sqrt(pt.log(visits.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / visits)
        a = pt.where(has_untried, a_new, pt.where(legal[s] > 0, ucb, NEG_INF).argmax(axis=1))
        on_path = active * (1.0 - at_terminal) # (node, a) is an edge of this path
        expanding = on_path * has_untried
        rng, s_next = rng.categorical(p=P[s, a])
        expand_node = pt.where(expanding > 0, node, expand_node)
        expand_action = pt.where(expanding > 0, a, expand_action)
        leaf = pt.where(active > 0, pt.where(expanding > 0, s_next, s), leaf)
        stop = pt.maximum(at_terminal, has_untried.astype("float64"))
        node_next = pt.where(active * (1.0 - stop) > 0, children[trees, node, a], node)
        return (
            rng,
            node_next,
            active * (1.0 - stop),
            expand_node,
            expand_action,
            leaf,
            node,
            a,
            on_path * reward[s, a],
            on_path,
            expanding
        )

    def iteration(i, rng, children, node_state, N, W, n_nodes):
        """One MCTS iteration in every tree: selection, expansion, simulation, backup.

        Parameters
        ----------
        i : TensorVariable of int, scalar
            The iteration number. Unused.
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        children, node_state, N, W
            The trees, as described in `select`.
        n_nodes : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            Nodes in each tree so far. The next new node gets this index.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, children, node_state, N, W, n_nodes
            The advanced generator and the grown trees.
        """
        zeros = pt.zeros((n_trees,), dtype="int64")

        # 1. selection
        (rng, _, _, expand_node_seq, expand_action_seq, leaf_seq,
         path_node, path_action, path_reward, on_path, expanding) = pytensor.scan(
            fn=select,
            outputs_info=[
                rng,
                zeros,
                pt.ones((n_trees,)),
                zeros,
                zeros,
                node_state[:, 0],
                None, None, None, None, None
            ],
            non_sequences=[children, node_state, N, W],
            n_steps=max_depth,
            return_updates=False
        )

        expand_node, expand_action, leaf = expand_node_seq[-1], expand_action_seq[-1], leaf_seq[-1]

        # 2. expansion
        expanded = expanding.sum(axis=0)
        children = pt.set_subtensor(
            children[trees, expand_node, expand_action],
            pt.where(expanded > 0, n_nodes, children[trees, expand_node, expand_action])
        )

        node_state = pt.set_subtensor(
            node_state[trees, n_nodes],
            pt.where(expanded > 0, leaf, node_state[trees, n_nodes])
        )

        n_nodes = n_nodes + expanded.astype("int64")

        # 3. simulation
        rng, G_leaf = random_rollout_returns(rng, leaf, tensors, gamma, horizon)

        # 4. backup: each edge's return, deepest first, then one scatter-add for the whole path
        def one_level_up(r, edge, G):
            "the return from one edge up: r + gamma * G on the path, unchanged off it"
            return pt.where(edge > 0, r + gamma * G, G)

        G_path = pytensor.scan(
            fn=one_level_up,
            sequences=[path_reward[::-1], on_path[::-1]],
            outputs_info=G_leaf,
            return_updates=False
        )
        G_path = G_path[::-1] # Reverse

        N = pt.inc_subtensor(N[trees[None, :], path_node, path_action], on_path)
        W = pt.inc_subtensor(W[trees[None, :], path_node, path_action], on_path * G_path)
        return rng, children, node_state, N, W, n_nodes

    rng_final, _, _, N_seq, W_seq, _ = pytensor.scan(
        fn=iteration,
        sequences=pt.arange(n_iterations),
        outputs_info=[
            rng_shared,
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity, n_actions), dtype="int64") - 1,
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity), dtype="int64") + roots[:, None],
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity, n_actions)),
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity, n_actions)),
            pt.ones((n_trees,), dtype="int64")
        ],
        return_updates=False
    )
    N_root, W_root = N_seq[-1][:, 0], W_seq[-1][:, 0]
    return pytensor.function(
        [roots],
        [N_root.argmax(axis=1), N_root, W_root / N_root],
        updates={rng_shared: rng_final}
    )
```

We run eight independent trees from every state, 296 trees in one batch, at four budgets, from 50 iterations (a tree of 51 nodes) up to 3,200.


```{python}

for n_iterations in (50, 200, 800, 3200):
    mcts = make_mcts(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF, HORIZON, MAX_DEPTH_MCTS, n_iterations, C_UCB, seed=811)
    actions, _, _ = mcts(roots_repeated_mcts)

policy_mcts = induced_policy(actions, roots_repeated_mcts, cliff)
```

**MCTS gets further than rollouts.** Its mean shortfall falls steadily as the budget grows, far past the $11.79$ that rollouts converge toward. At 3,200 iterations half of its choices are optimal (50.7%, against 28.6% for rollouts). Growing a tree toward good lines lets MCTS improve on its rollout policy by more than one step.

**But from starting state it still never finishes** ($v(S) = -20$). Looking inside the trees at two cells on the cliff edge shows where it goes wrong.


```{python}

    group = f"Row {edge_row}, column {column}: {n_cols_cliff - column} steps from the goal along the edge"

edge_table = (

    .tab_header(

    .fmt_markdown(columns="measure")
    .fmt_number(columns=action_columns, rows=rows_visits, decimals=0)
    .fmt_number(columns=action_columns, rows=rows_values, decimals=1)
    .cols_align("right", columns=action_columns)
    .tab_options(row_group_font_weight="bold", row_group_background_color="#f2f2f2")
)
edge_table
```

**Three steps from the goal, MCTS has found the way along the edge.** 3,149 of the 3,200 visits went right, and its estimate for that move, $-12.3$, is most of the way from what random rollouts alone would say ($q_{\text{random}} = -190.5$) to the true value ($q_* = -2.9$). The tree has grown along the edge all the way to the goal, so every iteration down that branch now reaches the goal within a few steps, instead of handing over to a random walk beside the cliff.

**Eight steps from the goal, it's a different story** "Up" gets 2,356 of the visits, and every action's mean return lies between $-139$ and $-352$. That is an order of magnitude away from $q_*$, and about the same size as $q_{\text{random}}$, implying that no iteration has yet followed the edge far enough to reach the goal before the random rollout took over.

The rollouts here are **deceptive**, not just noisy. From any cell next to the cliff, a random walk falls off a quarter of the time, so the edge *looks* catastrophic. The tree policy sensibly spends its visits away from the edge. However, that is exactly where the tree would have to grow to learn otherwise.

The averaging in the backup makes this trap hard to escape. An edge's value is the *mean* of every return that has ever passed through it, so the early, terrible rollout returns keep dragging down the path along the edge until enough good returns outnumber them. That is also why even the successful estimate above, $-12.3$, is still short of the true $-2.9$.


```{python}
planner_policies = {

    "MCTS, 3200 iterations": policy_mcts,

}

MOSTLY_OPTIMAL, MOSTLY_NOT = colors[0], colors[2] # cell fill colors: P(optimal action) >= 0.5 or < 0.5
labels_cliff = {start_cliff: "S", int(np.argmax(cliff.terminal)): "G"}
```

The figure above puts all three planners on one axis, computation per decision, and on that axis heuristic search looks absurdly cheap: depth 5 (1,364 tree nodes) beats MCTS at 3,200 iterations
(around 480,000 simulated transitions). But this is not a like-for-like comparison:

- **Heuristic search was given $v_{\text{random}}$ exactly**, at every leaf, for free. Computing it took a full DP solve on the distribution model (background planning) before the first decision was ever made.

- **The rollout algorithm and MCTS had only a sample model.** They had to estimate the same values by running the random policy, one noisy 150-step return at a time.

**The benefits of decision-time planning depends on the knowledge it starts from.** With a decent value function, a shallow search goes a long way. Without one, simulation has to pay for that knowledge, and the rollout policy decides whether the simulations even point in the right direction. On the cliff, random rollouts point the wrong way near the edge, so MCTS is only a middling planner here. Its strength is growing a tree toward promising path **when rollouts are at least roughly informative**. Its weakness, which we have just measured, is that averaged rollout
returns can hide a good path behind a first step that looks dangerous.

# Summary & Recap

Planning needs a model. It can be a **distribution model**, which lists every outcome and its probability, as DP uses, or a **sample model**, which produces one outcome at a time, as simulation
uses. The important idea is that planning and learning are the same computation applied to different experience, and we saw that with the Q-learning update, fed by a model, converged to $q_*$ without a single real episode, and Dyna-Q ran the identical update on real and simulated transitions inside one agent.

The rest of the chapter is about **where to spend the computation**:

| method | plans with |
|---|---|
| Q-planning | a given model |
| Dyna-Q | a learned table model |
| Dyna-Q+ | learned model + bonus $\kappa\sqrt\tau$ |
| prioritized sweeping | learned model + queue of predecessors |
| trajectory sampling | distribution model |
| RTDP | distribution model |
| heuristic search | distribution model + $v_{\text{random}}$ |
| rollouts | sample model + random policy |
| MCTS | sample model + random policy |

- **Planning is learning on simulated experience.** Random-sample one-step Q-planning is just Q-learning fed by a model. Given the distribution model, its updates became expected updates and
reached $q_*$ exactly. Given the sample model, they got close and then fluctuated in a noise band around $q_*$, whose width was set by the constant $\alpha$.

- **Dyna** learns and plans at the same time. On the Dyna maze, 50 planning steps per real step learned the maze in about 3 episodes, against 29 for plain Q-learning, because the model replays every rewarding transition until its value has spread backward along the path.

- **A model can be wrong in two ways.** Optimistic errors, where the model promises something the world no longer offers (the blocking maze), get corrected by experience. Pessimistic errors, where the model misses an improvement (the shortcut maze), do not: plain Dyna-Q never found the shortcut. Dyna-Q+'s $\kappa\sqrt\tau$ bonus found it, at the price of slightly less reward while nothing had changed.

- **Prioritized sweeping** works backward from the pairs whose values just changed. A priority *array* replaced the usual heap, a single mask replaced the lists of predecessors, and it needed 47-67 times fewer updates than Dyna-Q.

- **Sample vs expected updates.** The sample-error formula $\sqrt{(b-1)/bt}$ matched simulation to two decimal places. With a large branching factor $b$, a small fraction of one expected update's computation already removes most of the error.


- **Trajectory sampling** helped early on (most with small $b$ and large state spaces) and fell behind uniform sweeps later.

- **RTDP** left 73% of states with at most 10 updates, and its greedy policy became near-optimal from the start line. But on a track where half the reachable states are relevant, sweeping DP's *policy* was ready sooner.

- **Decision-time planning** on the cliff, all starting from the random policy: heuristic search fixed more states with each extra level of depth, starting nearest the goal, at an exponential cost; rollouts converged to exactly one step of policy iteration; MCTS got further, but its averaged random rollouts kept it away from the cliff edge.
